record.original_question: What is the maximum integer m for which there exists an equidistant permutation array with parameters (12,8,m), meaning an m x 12 matrix whose rows are permutations of 0 through 11 and such that every pair of distinct rows differs in exactly 8 positions?

evidence.quote: An "equidistant permutation array" (EPA) with parameters (n,d,m) can be represented as an m by n matrix (m rows and n columns), where each row is the permutation of the numbers 0 to n-1. Each pair of distinct rows must differ in exactly d positions. Given (n,d,m), we want to construct an equidistant permutation array (EPA) with these parameters.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An equidistant permutation array with parameters $(n,d,m)$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose entries are integers in $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, such that every row is a permutation of $0,1,\dots,n-1$, and every pair of distinct rows differs in exactly $d$ column positions (equivalently, agrees in exactly $n-d$ positions).

Determine the largest integer $m$ for which there exists an equidistant permutation array with parameters $(n,d,m) = (12,8,m)$.
artifact.status_search_result: The exact maximum size of an equidistant permutation array with parameters (12,8) does not appear to be established in the literature. Searches return general work on bounds and constructions for equidistant permutation arrays, but no resolved value for (12,8). Recent computational work has improved the lower bound to m ≥ 21, but no matching upper bound is known, so the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: On Maximal Equidistant Permutation Arrays
status_evidence.snippet: Studies maximal equidistant permutation arrays and their bounds, without resolving the (12,8) case.
status_evidence.claim: General bounds on maximum sizes of equidistant permutation arrays are studied but the (12,8) case is not resolved.

status_evidence.title: Equidistant permutation arrays: a bound
status_evidence.snippet: Provides bounds for equidistant permutation arrays.
status_evidence.claim: Known bounds do not pin down the maximum m for (12,8).
